paras: The Lenox Hotel shooting took place on the night of May 2, 1903, in New York City, when three off-duty policemen beat Jefferson Sanders, a Black waiter, with their revolvers in the "black and tan" saloon where he worked, and Sanders shot all three. Patrolman Ernest O. J. Peters and Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley died, while Patrolman Joseph Russo survived. Witnesses said the policemen began the attack, a grand jury declined to indict Sanders, and Black newspapers held up his act as justified self-defense.

Gilhooley (also Gilhooly), Peters and Russo belonged to Inspector Kane's staff in Queens and had marched in the police parade that day; Kane said they had no reason to be in the resort. Sanders, about fifty, had worked at the hotel, at Sixth Avenue and Third Street, for five years; the police said he had served long terms in Sing Sing, and he said he had lived honestly since his release.

In Sanders's account, Gilhooley said, "We'll have a muss with these coons before we leave," and when Sanders started out to find a policeman, Peters cursed him and struck him in the mouth. The three then pinned him against a radiator and pounded his head with their revolver butts, he said, and the bartender, James Franklin, gave a matching account. Patrolman Rudolph Beyers, who came in from the street, later testified that Gilhooly had his revolver pointed at Sanders.

Sanders then fired five shots, the first inside and the rest on the sidewalk, according to the cashier, Abraham Peters. Peters died as the ambulance pulled away, Gilhooley died the next evening, and Russo recovered from a lung wound. Beyers clubbed Sanders while disarming him, and as white and Black residents gathered the Tribune wrote that "it was feared there would be a race riot."

Sanders was held without bail on May 3 while a crowd around the patrol wagon seemed ready to assault him, according to the Tribune. The Tombs physician found his scalp covered with wounds, and thousands attended Gilhooly's funeral. At the May 18 inquest the cashier said he saw Sanders do nothing to justify the assault, but the jury found that Sanders had inflicted the fatal wounds and he was committed to the Tombs.

On August 17 the grand jury failed to indict, and Recorder Goff set Sanders free. Assistant District Attorney Perkins said the evidence showed Gilhooley attacked Sanders, who drew only after being beaten and after the policemen had drawn. The Evening World said the Police Department had considered a conviction certain; no report of discipline against Russo was found.

The Tribune called Sanders a "negro ex-convict" and quoted police calling him a "bad negro," yet headlined "Witnesses Say Prisoner Was First Attacked" and printed his statement at length. The Associated Press night dispatch also led with the witnesses, under headlines such as "Opened Fire on His Tormentors" in Worcester and "Policemen to Blame" in Portland, Maine. The next day's wire added the police label "bad nigger," and some papers chose headlines like "Negro's Aim Was True" and "Colored Desperado Kills Two." In August the wire opened with Sanders "terribly beaten" before he fired, and the Tribune headlined "Killed to Save Self."

Black newspapers took Sanders's side. The Colored American's editorial "An Eye for an Eye" called him the "patient and courteous waiter," found his act "justifiable," and proposed "remember Gilhooly!" as a warning to white men. The Cleveland Gazette said he was beaten "all on account of his being a colored man" and urged readers to defend themselves with Winchesters. The Indianapolis Freeman cited the case against brutality by Irish New York policemen, while the American Baptist called the shooting self-defense yet said Sanders "caused the race riot."

Sanders, the saloon witnesses and the district attorney said the policemen started the fight. Coroner Scholer cited a "good source" that Sanders was offered $20 to "do up" the policemen, and the Evening World noted an unattributed story that Sanders was drunk and fired first. The police also said only Gilhooly carried a pistol, and a hospital surgeon found no liquor on the wounded men, against witnesses who said they had been drinking.

bases: Three off-duty policemen in plain clothes beat Jefferson Sanders, a Black waiter, with revolver butts in the saloon where he worked, and a uniformed patrolman clubbed him as he was disarmed; Sanders shot all three (A2, A22, A23, A25).

accounts.label: Sanders's statement
accounts.gist: Gilhooley said they would 'have a muss with these coons'; Peters cursed and struck him; the three chased him, pinned him to a radiator and beat him with revolver butts; not knowing they were police, he shot in fear for his life.

accounts.label: Saloon witnesses and inquest testimony
accounts.gist: The cashier and bartender said the three policemen began the beating with revolver butts and Sanders seemed to be defending himself; Beyers said Gilhooly had a revolver pointed at Sanders.

accounts.label: Russo's statement
accounts.gist: They stopped only to use the toilet room; he heard a dispute, went to the back room, saw a scuffle and was shot; he did not see how it began.

accounts.label: Police and Coroner's claims
accounts.gist: Police called Sanders a 'bad negro' with a long prison record; Coroner Scholer cited an unnamed source that Sanders was offered $20 to 'do up' the policemen; a second story held he was drunk and quarrelsome and fired before the police drew.

accounts.label: District attorney after the grand jury
accounts.gist: The evidence showed Sanders was badly beaten before he shot and Gilhooly drew a weapon first.

accounts.label: Black editorialists
accounts.gist: The policemen, drunk and abusive, attacked a peaceful waiter because he was Black, and his shooting was justified self-defense.

framing.detail: The Tribune called him a 'negro ex-convict' and the police's 'bad negro' but headlined 'Witnesses Say Prisoner Was First Attacked' and printed his statement at length.
The AP night wire led with witnesses blaming the police ('Opened fire on his tormentors', 'Policemen to Blame').
The AP follow-up repeated the police's 'bad nigger' label; some headlines read 'Negro's Aim Was True' and 'Colored Desperado Kills Two'.
August reports of the release led with Sanders 'terribly beaten' before he fired; the Tribune headlined 'Killed to Save Self'.
The Colored American's 'An Eye for an Eye' found the act 'justifiable' and mocked the police as 'guardians (?) of the law'.
The Cleveland Gazette and the Freeman cited the case to urge armed self-defense against white attackers and police.
The American Baptist called it self-defense yet said Sanders 'caused the race riot'.

versions.value: The policemen, unprovoked (Sanders, cashier, bartender, AP witnesses, district attorney)

info: Night of Saturday, May 2, 1903, after the police parade
Lenox Hotel, a 'black and tan' saloon at Sixth Avenue and Third Street, Manhattan, and the sidewalk outside
Jefferson Sanders (also 'Saunders'; 'Joseph Saunders' in the Cleveland Gazette), Black waiter or bouncer, about 50, beaten about the head

Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley (Gilhooly), Patrolman Ernest O. J. Peters and Patrolman/Detective Joseph Russo of Inspector Kane's staff, Queens, off duty and in plain clothes; Patrolman Rudolph Beyers (Byers) of the Mercer Street station clubbed Sanders while disarming him
Sanders released by Recorder Goff in the Court of General Sessions
